raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to overcome perceived limitations of permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): chronic caging of the vessel, impaired vasomotion, late neoatherosclerosis, side-branch jailing, and a substrate for very late stent thrombosis. The concept is not new. The Igaki-Tamai poly-L-lactic acid scaffold established the feasibility of temporary coronary scaffolding in humans [1], and long-term follow-up suggested that complete disappearance of the device could be compatible with durable clinical safety [2]. The modern field, however, was defined by the everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold, a thick-strut polymeric platform designed to provide early radial support and drug delivery, followed by hydrolytic resorption over several years [3].

Early single-arm Absorb studies were encouraging. First-in-human data showed acceptable acute performance and late lumen stability [3], with serial imaging suggesting restoration of vasomotion and progressive reduction in scaffold footprint [4]. Iteration of scaffold design improved radial strength and deployment reliability [5], and longer multimodality imaging follow-up supported the appealing biological narrative of “vascular restoration therapy” [6]. These studies were small, highly selected, and performed by expert operators, but they generated the rationale for randomized trials against contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic DES.

The randomized evidence was sobering. ABSORB II showed similar early clinical outcomes but failed to demonstrate superiority for vasomotion or late luminal enlargement, and at 3 years reported excess device-oriented events and scaffold thrombosis [7], [8]. ABSORB III met its primary non-inferiority endpoint at 1 year in relatively simple lesions, but event curves subsequently diverged, particularly for target-vessel myocardial infarction and thrombosis [9]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China broadly confirmed comparable early angiographic efficacy in selected patients, while still showing numerically higher thrombotic risk with BVS [10], [11]. In a more pragmatic setting, AIDA was stopped early because definite or probable scaffold thrombosis was significantly increased compared with metallic DES [12]. ABSORB IV, designed with improved lesion selection and implantation technique, reduced but did not eliminate safety concerns [13]. COMPARE-ABSORB further emphasized that in higher-risk clinical and angiographic subsets the first-generation polymeric BVS could not match contemporary metallic DES [14].

Meta-analyses clarified the signal. Trial-level and patient-level analyses consistently demonstrated higher definite or probable thrombosis, target-lesion failure, and myocardial infarction with Absorb compared with everolimus-eluting metallic DES, particularly during the first 3 years, the period before substantial scaffold resorption [15], [16]. Longer follow-up suggested that the excess hazard attenuates after bioresorption, supporting the original biological premise but not offsetting early harm for a first-generation device [17].

Mechanistic studies identified several contributors. Thick struts impaired deliverability and flow, required meticulous lesion preparation, and increased malapposition risk in small vessels. Optical coherence tomography and pathology studies of late and very late scaffold thrombosis showed underexpansion, uncovered or malapposed struts, discontinuity, peri-strut low-intensity areas, dismantling, and neoatherosclerosis [18], [19]. A systematic review of very late events reinforced that thrombosis was often multifactorial and related both to implantation and to scaffold degradation biology [20].

Technique therefore became central. The “PSP” approach—adequate predilatation, appropriate vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—was associated with improved acute expansion and lower adverse events [21]. Registry and pooled analyses suggested that avoiding small reference vessels and ensuring optimal expansion reduced scaffold thrombosis, although such strategies could not fully normalize outcomes [22], [23]. BVS performance in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction was initially attractive because younger patients and softer plaques might benefit from temporary scaffolding; TROFI II and related studies showed acceptable healing but did not establish clear clinical superiority [24], [25].

The field has since shifted from enthusiasm for first-generation Absorb to cautious redesign. Magnesium-based scaffolds offer thinner struts, improved radial properties, faster resorption, and potentially more favorable healing. BIOSOLVE-I established feasibility of a drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffold [26], and BIOSOLVE-II showed improved angiographic and clinical performance of the second-generation device [27]. Larger BIOSOLVE-IV data suggested encouraging safety, though randomized comparisons with best-in-class DES and longer follow-up remain essential [28]. Other polymeric platforms such as DESolve demonstrated the possibility of self-correction and alternative resorption profiles, but clinical adoption remained limited [29].

Current clinical lessons are clear. First-generation Absorb BVS should not be considered equivalent to contemporary metallic DES for routine PCI. The excess early thrombotic risk arose from the interaction of device design, lesion selection, deployment technique, and resorption behavior. Nevertheless, the concept remains scientifically compelling: if a scaffold can provide safe early support, deliver antiproliferative therapy, and then disappear without late inflammation or dismantling, it could benefit selected younger patients, diffuse disease requiring future surgical options, or lesions where restoration of physiology matters. Future BVS development must prioritize thinner struts, predictable degradation, radiographic visibility, wider expansion latitude, simpler implantation, and rigorous randomized evaluation against modern ultrathin DES [30].
